title: MA9-06799
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXXX XXXXXX XXXX, his wife, XXXX XXXXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, and their three minor sons, XXXX XXXX XXXXXXX XXXXXX, XXXXXXX XXXXXXX XXXXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXXXXX XXXXXX, all citizens of Mexico, are claiming refugee protection in Canada under section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA). The father, XXXX XXXXX XXXXXX XXXX, was appointed as the designated representative of his minor children.

The principal claimant alleged that in XXXX 2008, a municipal police commander in XXXXXX (XXXX XXXX) tried to recruit him for an intimidation operation, and that he refused. As a result, he was viciously attacked and beaten by police officers. This was done as a reprisal, but also to persuade the principal claimant to participate in their crimes. A little later, police officers tried again and threatened him if he did not agree to collaborate with them. The principal claimant and his family moved into his mother-in-law's home and remained in hiding there for some time. Fearing for their safety, the entire family came to Canada and claimed refugee protection on their arrival at the Montréal airport on XXXXX, 2008.
The claimants are not "Convention refugees" under section 96 of the IRPA or "persons in need of protection" under subsection 97(1) of the Act, for the reasons that follow.
The claimants' identities were established to the panel's satisfaction by the documents submitted on file.1 CLAIM UNDER SECTION 96 OF THE IRPA

The claimants produced no evidence of persecution in connection with their race, nationality, religion or political opinion. In response to question 28 on their Personal Information Forms (PIFs), the claimants stated that they fear persecution because of their membership in a particular social group. However, they were threatened in the context of non-political crimes, not on any of the Convention grounds. The evidence does not establish their membership in a particular social group, within the meaning of Ward,2 and the panel is therefore of the opinion that the claimants were not persecuted because of their membership in a particular social group. The panel therefore determines that the claim cannot be allowed under section 96 of the IRPA. CLAIM UNDER PARAGRAPH 97(1)(a)

The claimants produced no evidence that they could face a danger of torture within the meaning of Article 1 of the Convention Against Torture should they return to their country. Consequently, the panel determines that the claim cannot be allowed under paragraph 97(1)(a) of the IRPA. CLAIM UNDER PARAGRAPH 97(1)(b)

At the hearing, the principal claimant contradicted the content of his PIF, in particular when he maintained that he had been beaten twice, whereas his response to question 31 mentions only one incident of this kind; when he stated that he had been stopped and threatened by police officers, whereas this incident is not included in his narrative; and when he stated that he had moved in with his mother-in-law in approximately XXXX 2008, whereas his response to question 11 of his PIF indicates XXXXX 2007. Because of these contradictions, as well as the inconsistency of the principal claimant's testimony, the panel finds them to be not credible.

The male claimant confirmed in his testimony that he had never filed a complaint at the state level in XXXXX XXXX, or at the federal level, against the municipal police commander who he alleges was the agent of harm. Although the panel understands the fears relating to the lack of integrity of some Mexican police forces, beyond his mere perceptions, the claimant did not produce clear and convincing evidence to establish why he could not have obtained protection in his country had he gone to the competent authorities. As such, the panel is of the opinion that he failed in his duty to make the efforts that are expected of a claimant, to seek protection in his country of nationality before seeking international protection.

Despite this, the panel will spend no further time supporting the above arguments, as it has concluded that an internal flight alternative (IFA) is available to the claimant. This, as we know, is a determinative consideration in any claim for refugee protection, and "is in itself sufficient to dispose of the refugee claim", as the Honourable Justice Shore stated in Palacios.3

At the hearing, the principal claimant was asked about what he and his family would fear if they were to move to another part of the country, such as Merida (Yucatán) or La Paz (Baja California Sur). Although the panel gave them the opportunity to support their evidence, the claimants produced no actual, concrete evidence, and gave no probative reasons, within the meaning of the case law,4 to show why it would be unreasonable for them to seek refuge in one of these cities, or why there might be conditions that would, on a balance of probabilities, give rise to a risk to their lives or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment, should they move there.

The principal claimant cited the fact that the alleged agent of harm would find him wherever he went in Mexico and that, because of this, he could be killed. However, the panel is of the opinion that, beyond speculation and vague impressions, he produced no actual, concrete evidence establishing a risk to the claimants' lives or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment at the level of a balance of probabilities.

In the case at bar, the panel is of the opinion that the claimants have not discharged their burden of proof, as established by the case law,5 to demonstrate that no IFA is available to them, in either Merida (Yucatán) or La Paz (Baja California Sur), should they return to their country. As Justice Lagacé stated in Ramirez:6 "...the burden of proof regarding an internal flight alternative rests on the claimant... Thus, the applicant had to establish either that it would be unreasonable for her to seek refuge in another part of the country or that there were, in fact, conditions preventing her from relocating elsewhere in Mexico..."

In light of the foregoing analysis, the panel is of the opinion that IFAs are available to the claimants. The panel therefore determines that the claim for refugee protection cannot be allowed under subsection 97(1) of the IRPA.

For the foregoing reasons, the panel rejects these claims for refugee protection. The claimants are not "Convention refugees" under section 96 of the IRPA or "persons in need of protection" under subsection 97(1) of the Act.
